sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Caching is the technique of storing frequently accessed data in a faster, closer medium (memory instead of disk, edge instead of origin) so that subsequent reads complete in microseconds instead of milliseconds — reducing latency, lowering database load, and cutting infrastructure cost.

Caching exists because of one brutal fact of systems design: **storage is a hierarchy, and every level is 10×–1000× slower than the one above it**. A modern CPU register returns data in ~0.3 nanoseconds; L1 cache in ~1 ns; L2 in ~4 ns; L3 in ~12 ns; main memory (RAM) in ~100 ns; an SSD in ~100 μs; a rotating disk in ~10 ms; and a network round-trip to another datacenter in ~30 ms. Each step down the pyramid costs roughly an order of magnitude, which means a single disk read is the equivalent of ~100,000 L1 cache hits. Caching is simply the deliberate act of moving hot data up the pyramid so that the overwhelmingly common read path stays on the fast levels. Real-world: Facebook's memcached layer runs tens of thousands of cache nodes answering billions of reads per second — without it, their MySQL backend would need to be hundreds of times larger, and the newsfeed would arrive in seconds instead of milliseconds.

The **first** reason to cache is **latency reduction**. When a Netflix user clicks a title, the playback service must resolve the user's profile, language preferences, parental controls, resume position, and personalized artwork within ~200 ms or the click feels sluggish. Fetching each of these from a relational database across a network hop would blow the budget before the stream even begins. By placing that data in Redis co-located with the playback service, each lookup becomes a sub-millisecond `GET`, and the entire profile assembly completes in single-digit milliseconds. The same pattern drives Instagram's feed rendering, Uber's surge-pricing lookups, and YouTube's video metadata resolution — every consumer-facing product with a strict latency SLO uses an in-memory cache as the first hop.

The **second** reason is **database load reduction**. Databases are expensive to scale horizontally (sharding introduces consistency trade-offs, replicas have lag, distributed transactions are slow), but they are also the slowest component in most stacks. A single Postgres instance might handle 5,000 queries per second before connection exhaustion and lock contention set in, yet the application in front of it may need to serve 50,000 reads per second during a peak. Caching absorbs the read fan-out: if the cache hit rate is 90%, the database sees only 5,000 qps; at 99% hit rate, the database sees 500 qps. Amazon's product-detail page is the canonical example — the page is assembled from dozens of services, but the catalog data (title, price, image URL, bullet points) is served from a multi-tier cache (CDN edge → regional ElastiCache → DynamoDB), and the database behind it only sees a small trickle of misses. Without the cache, DynamoDB would need to be provisioned at 10–50× the capacity, multiplying cost proportionally.

The **third** reason is **cost savings**. RAM is more expensive than SSD per gigabyte, but a single Redis instance can serve 100,000 reads per second for ~$200/month, while a Postgres instance serving the same QPS from disk would cost thousands and still be slower. The math is straightforward: if hot data is 1% of total data, caching that 1% in RAM eliminates 90%+ of database load at a fraction of the cost. WhatsApp's message-read-status system caches the last-seen timestamps of billions of users in a small set of Redis shards; reading these from Cassandra would require a full-table lookup per message-send, multiplying cluster cost by an order of magnitude. Netflix's recommendation service precomputes personalized rows for each user during off-peak hours, caches them in EVCache (their memcached fork), and serves 100% of peak traffic from cache — letting the recommendation backend run on a tiny fraction of the fleet.

The **memory hierarchy** in a typical web service has four tiers, each adding capacity at the cost of latency. The **browser cache** (HTTP `Cache-Control`, ETags) eliminates the request entirely — a returning YouTube viewer gets the thumbnail from disk for free. The **CDN edge** (Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront) terminates requests near the user — Netflix Open Connect appliances sit inside ISP datacenters, serving video bytes without crossing the public internet. The **application cache** (Redis, memcached) sits next to the service — Netflix's EVCache answers profile and metadata reads in under 1 ms. Finally, the **database buffer pool** (PostgreSQL `shared_buffers`, InnoDB `innodb_buffer_pool`) is the last line of defense — frequently-accessed disk pages live in RAM, so even "disk reads" usually don't hit the spindle. A well-designed read path traverses these tiers in order and short-circuits at the first hit; a poorly designed path bypasses them and pays full price on every read.

Caching's trade-offs are real and must not be hand-waved. **Stale data** is the headline risk: any cached value can lag behind the source of truth, and the longer the TTL, the staler it gets. **Cache stampede** (thundering herd) happens when a popular key expires and thousands of concurrent requests miss simultaneously and hammer the database. **Consistency** becomes harder: a write that updates the DB but fails to invalidate the cache leaves stale data serving reads until TTL. **Memory pressure** is constant — caches must have eviction policies (LRU, LFU, TTL) or they will OOM. And **operational complexity** grows: every cache is one more distributed system to monitor, size, fail over, and reason about. The Netflix Chaos Monkey famously kills cache nodes in production precisely to force engineers to design for cache failure — because caches *will* fail, and the database must be able to absorb the resulting load spike.

When used well, caching is the highest-leverage optimization in distributed systems. It turns a 50 ms database read into a 0.5 ms cache read, a $50,000/month database cluster into a $5,000/month cache + $5,000/month database pair, and a fragile system that buckles under load into one that gracefully absorbs spikes. The rest of this phase covers the canonical cache patterns — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead, eviction, and consistency — each of which trades a different combination of latency, freshness, complexity, and correctness.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Client["Client request"] Client --> Browser["Browser cache
(disk, ms)"] Browser -->|miss| CDN["CDN edge
(PoP, ~5-20 ms)"] CDN -->|miss| AppCache["App cache: Redis/memcached
(RAM, <1 ms)"] AppCache -->|miss| DBBuffer["DB buffer pool
(RAM, ~1 ms)"] DBBuffer -->|miss| Disk["SSD / disk
(100 μs - 10 ms)"] Disk -->|miss| Cold["Cold storage / archive
(seconds-minutes)"] Browser -.->|"hit ~0 ms"| Done1["Response sent"] CDN -.->|"hit ~10 ms"| Done2["Response sent"] AppCache -.->|"hit ~0.5 ms"| Done3["Response sent"] DBBuffer -.->|"hit ~1 ms"| Done4["Response sent"] Hierarchy["Memory hierarchy (latency pyramid)"] Hierarchy --> Reg["CPU register: 0.3 ns"] Hierarchy --> L1["L1 cache: 1 ns"] Hierarchy --> L2["L2 cache: 4 ns"] Hierarchy --> L3["L3 cache: 12 ns"] Hierarchy --> RAM["Main memory: 100 ns"] Hierarchy --> SSD["SSD: 100 μs"] Hierarchy --> HDD["HDD: 10 ms"] Hierarchy --> Net["Network DC-DC: 30 ms"] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` Latency Pyramid (each tier ~10x slower) +---------+ | Register| 0.3 ns +---------+ | +------+------+ | L1 cache | 1 ns +-------------+ | +------+------+ | L2 cache | 4 ns +-------------+ | +------+------+ | L3 cache | 12 ns +-------------+ | +------+------+ | Main memory | 100 ns <-- Redis/memcached live here +-------------+ | +------+------+ | SSD | 100 us <-- DB on fast disk +-------------+ | +------+------+ | HDD | 10 ms <-- cold storage +-------------+ | +------+------+ | Network | 30 ms <-- cross-DC round trip +-------------+ Read path in a typical web service: Client | v +------------------+ hit (~0 ms) +----------+ | Browser cache |----------------->| Response | +------------------+ +----------+ | miss v +------------------+ hit (~10 ms) +----------+ | CDN edge node |----------------->| Response | +------------------+ +----------+ | miss v +------------------+ hit (~0.5 ms) +----------+ | Redis/memcached |----------------->| Response | +------------------+ +----------+ | miss v +------------------+ hit (~1 ms) +----------+ | DB buffer pool |----------------->| Response | +------------------+ +----------+ | miss v +------------------+ ~5-100 ms +----------+ | SSD / disk |----------------->| Response | +------------------+ +----------+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client issues a read (e.g., `GET /product/42`). The browser checks its HTTP cache; on a hit the request never leaves the device and the response is instant. 2. On a browser miss, the request reaches a CDN edge node. If the edge has a cached copy (validated via ETag/Cache-Control), it returns the bytes from a PoP near the user — typically 5–20 ms. 3. On a CDN miss, the request reaches the application tier. The service first checks Redis (or memcached); a hit returns in under 1 ms because the data is in RAM and the network hop is intra-datacenter. 4. On a cache miss, the service queries the database. The database's own buffer pool may already hold the relevant pages in RAM (1 ms), avoiding an actual disk read; only true cold reads reach the SSD (~100 μs) or disk (~10 ms). 5. After a database hit, the application back-fills the cache so the next read terminates one tier earlier. The cache hit rate determines how often the expensive tiers are touched — 99% means the database sees only 1% of reads.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Benchmark: in-memory dict lookup vs SQLite disk read.
# Demonstrates why caching exists: memory is ~1000x faster than disk.

import sqlite3
import time
import random
import statistics
from contextlib import contextmanager

N_ROWS = 50_000           # rows in the 'products' table
N_LOOKUPS = 10_000        # number of random lookups per scenario

# ---------- Set up an on-disk SQLite database ----------
def build_db(path="/tmp/products.db"):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path)
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS products")
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price REAL)")
    conn.executemany(
        "INSERT INTO products VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        [(i, f"product-{i}", round(random.random() * 100, 2)) for i in range(N_ROWS)],
    )
    conn.commit()
    return conn

# ---------- Timed context manager ----------
@contextmanager
def timed(label, samples):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    yield
    elapsed_us = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1_000_000
    samples.append(elapsed_us)
    print(f"{label:35s}  total={elapsed_us:10.0f} us   "
          f"avg={elapsed_us / N_LOOKUPS:8.2f} us/op")

def bench_disk(conn):
    """Every lookup is a real SQLite read (bypassing our own cache)."""
    samples = []
    with timed("SQLite disk reads (cold, no cache)", samples):
        for _ in range(N_LOOKUPS):
            pid = random.randrange(N_ROWS)
            cur = conn.execute("SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE id=?", (pid,))
            cur.fetchone()
    return samples[0]

def bench_dict_cache(conn):
    """Pre-load all rows into an in-memory dict, then look up."""
    cache = {row[0]: (row[1], row[2]) for row in
             conn.execute("SELECT id, name, price FROM products")}
    samples = []
    with timed("In-memory dict lookups (cache hit)", samples):
        for _ in range(N_LOOKUPS):
            pid = random.randrange(N_ROWS)
            _ = cache[pid]
    return samples[0]

def bench_with_buffer_pool(conn):
    """Second pass on disk: SQLite's pager now has hot pages in memory."""
    samples = []
    with timed("SQLite disk reads (warm buffer pool)", samples):
        for _ in range(N_LOOKUPS):
            pid = random.randrange(N_ROWS)
            cur = conn.execute("SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE id=?", (pid,))
            cur.fetchone()
    return samples[0]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    conn = build_db()
    # Warm SQLite's internal pager so disk reads on the second pass are fair.
    list(conn.execute("SELECT * FROM products"))

    print(f"\nBenchmark: {N_LOOKUPS} random lookups over {N_ROWS} rows\n" + "-" * 70)
    disk_cold_us = bench_disk(conn)
    disk_warm_us = bench_with_buffer_pool(conn)
    cache_us     = bench_dict_cache(conn)

    print("-" * 70)
    print(f"Speedup: dict cache vs cold disk = {disk_cold_us / cache_us:,.0f}x")
    print(f"Speedup: dict cache vs warm disk = {disk_warm_us / cache_us:,.0f}x")
    print("\nThis is why caching exists: memory hierarchy is logarithmic in cost.")
    conn.close()
```
